1: Open with a question: “Who has had a client say ‘we love them, but we’ve got no headcount’ in the last month?” Most hands go up. Every one of those conversations was a possible contract deal. This session teaches perm consultants to recognise those moments, understand how clients actually pay for people, and bring the contract team in at the right time. Ideally co-run with a contract manager.
2: Check the pre-work: everyone should have one real client who said “no headcount”. You’ll use them in the exercise.
3: The most common way a perm consultant loses a client is by hearing “no headcount” and walking away. Meanwhile the work still needs doing, and another agency or a systems integrator fills the gap. Spotting a contract need keeps you in the account and positions Stott and May as a partner across every hiring model. And a client who buys contract today is likely to buy perm from us later: winning together as one team grows the whole account. Five minutes.
4: Start with the basics; many perm consultants have never seen a contract deal run. The client pays Stott and May an hourly or daily rate for the contractor’s time. We engage and pay the contractor (on our payroll as a W-2 employee, or via their own company) and invoice the client, usually weekly from approved timesheets. Unlike perm, the relationship doesn’t end at placement: the contract team manages the contractor throughout, handles extensions and often places more people on the same project. Ask a contract consultant to walk through a real (anonymised) deal from first call to first invoice. Eight minutes.
5: The key row is “budget line”. A perm hire needs an approved headcount slot. A contractor is usually paid from a different pot: a project budget or a non-headcount line. That’s why a client can have a hiring freeze and still bring in contractors. The “who decides” row matters too: contract decisions often sit with whoever owns the project budget, which may not be the person you speak to on perm. Ask the contract team to add desk-specific examples. Eight minutes.
6: T&M means time and materials: the client pays for hours or days worked. An SOW (statement of work) is outcome-based: the client pays for a defined deliverable, and the delivery risk sits with us. Contract-to-hire is the natural bridge for perm consultants: the client gets the person now and converts later. The conversion fee and timing are agreed in the contract terms; check our standard terms with the contract team before quoting anything. Five minutes.
7: Contract supplies skills; consulting supplies an outcome. Under a statement of work (SOW) the client pays for a defined deliverable or a managed team, and Stott and May Consulting takes responsibility for delivery. This suits clients who don’t want to manage individual contractors, or who are frustrated with a systems integrator. Consulting engagements are often larger and longer, and they put us at the heart of the client’s transformation, which leads to perm and contract demand later. Perm consultants don’t need to scope or price it: spot the signal and bring in the consulting team. Ask the consulting team for one short case study to share here. Eight minutes.
8: The figures are illustrative only, not our actual rates or margins. The point is that contract earns on every hour worked, for as long as the contractor stays, and extensions are common. The gross spread is before employer costs: on W-2 that includes payroll taxes, insurance and benefits, which is why net margin is lower. W-2 means the contractor is employed through us; 1099 means an independent contractor; Corp-to-Corp (C2C) means they bill through their own company. Misclassification carries real legal risk, so perm consultants should never quote rates or promise a classification: bring in the contract team. Eight minutes.
9: Keep this simple. CapEx is money spent creating a long-term asset; the cost is capitalised and spread (depreciated or amortized) over its useful life. OpEx is the cost of running the business, expensed in the year it’s incurred. Under US accounting rules, some labour spent building internal software during the development phase can be capitalised, which is one reason big technology, data and ERP programmes often have capital budgets that pay for contractors and consultants. Contractors can also sit in OpEx, in a non-headcount or “contingent labour” line. Important: we never tell a client how to classify a cost. That’s their finance team’s decision. Our job is to ask which budget the work sits in. Ten minutes; check understanding by asking two people to explain it back in one sentence each.
10: These questions belong in every perm intake call (Module 04), not just when a role stalls. Question 5 is the most powerful: it makes the hiring manager say out loud what the empty seat is costing them, which is exactly the case for a contractor. Question 3 often leads you to a new stakeholder, such as a programme director or a finance business partner, who controls a bigger budget than your hiring manager. Pairs practise asking all six in a natural order, five minutes.
11: Group the signals into three families: budget (the money is somewhere other than headcount), time (the need is urgent or finite) and team (the gap is temporary or uncertain). Any one is worth a question; two or more together is a strong contract opportunity. Ask the room: which of these have you heard in the last month and walked past? Have each person pick their pre-work client and name the signals present. “Try before we commit” is the opening for contract-to-hire. Ten minutes.
12: Each reframe turns the objection into a question about cost, timing or budget, which brings you back to the funding questions. On “too expensive”: an hourly rate looks higher than a salary divided by hours, but it doesn’t carry a placement fee, benefits, onboarding or the cost of a long-term mis-hire, and it stops when the work stops. Don’t quote numbers you can’t back up. Pairs drill all four, rotating, five minutes.
13: The perm consultant doesn’t need to sell the contract deal alone. Their job is to spot it, open the door and book the joint call. Model the script, then have each person rewrite it in their own words using their pre-work client.
14: This is about working and winning together as one team. When a perm consultant opens the door to contract, the client gets the right solution now, and Stott and May becomes their partner across every hiring model. Clients who buy contract from us are likely to come back to us for perm later down the line, so staying close to the account pays off for everyone. The perm consultant keeps the relationship warm, joins the first call and stays in touch; the contract consultant runs the delivery. Agree who sends what to the client so the message stays consistent.
15: Prepare client cards in advance. Example: “You have a perm Data Engineer role on hold because of a headcount freeze. Your data platform migration goes live in eight weeks and you have a programme budget your director controls. Only reveal the budget if asked who owns it.” The trainee wins if they uncover the project budget and book a joint call with the contract team. Rotate roles so everyone plays all three.
16: Ask each person to name the client from their pre-work they’ll call back this week with the funding questions. Managers: track cross-desk leads logged and joint calls booked in the weekly activity review.
17: Open the floor for questions. Invite a contract consultant to answer desk-specific questions about rates, terms and availability.
